title: Subspaces, quotients and Baire category
summary: Closed subspaces of Banach spaces; quotient spaces and the quotient norm; seminorms and their null spaces; the Baire category theorem and its first consequence, the uniform boundedness principle.

objectives.description: Prove that a subspace of a Banach space is itself Banach exactly when it is closed, and exhibit a dense proper subspace.
Define the quotient of a normed space by a closed subspace and explain why the quotient norm is a norm.
State the Baire category theorem precisely and use it to show a Banach space has no countable Hamel basis.
State the uniform boundedness principle with its completeness hypothesis and give an example showing the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

preparation.description: Read lecture 3 notes page 1: subspaces (Definition 29), Proposition 30 (Banach iff closed) and the quotient space (Definition 31).
Read Example 32 and Theorem 33 on seminorms and the quotient by the null space (page 2).
Read Theorem 34 (Baire Category Theorem) with its proof (page 3), then Theorem 36 (Uniform Boundedness) with its proof (page 4).

activities.title: Lecture 3: subspaces, quotients, Baire
activities.instructions: Read the lesson with lecture 3 of the notes. After the statement of Baire's theorem, write down in your own words what 'nowhere dense' means before reading the proof.

activities.title: Tutorial: closed subspaces and Baire category
activities.instructions: Attempt exercises 1 and 2. Exercise 2 is the first genuine use of Baire's theorem; be explicit about which sets are closed and why they have empty interior.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A subspace of a Banach space is automatically complete because the big space is.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Only closed subspaces inherit completeness. The polynomials form a dense proper subspace of C([0,1]) and are not complete in the sup norm.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Baire's theorem says a complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It can (ℝ is a countable union of closed intervals). The theorem says at least one of the closed sets must contain an open ball; equivalently, a countable union of nowhere dense sets has empty interior.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Pointwise boundedness of operators always gives uniform boundedness.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Only on a Banach domain. On the incomplete space of finitely supported sequences, T_n(x) = n x_n is pointwise bounded but ‖T_n‖ = n.
